content: Preparation for Birth and Emergency Planning: 1. Essential Supplies for Birth: Have clean cloths of various sizes ready for different purposes: covering the bed, drying and wrapping the baby, cleaning the baby’s eyes, and for use as sanitary pads. Prepare warm covers for both the mother and the baby. Ensure a warm, clean surface or clean cloth is available for the birth. Have at least three bowls: two for washing and one for the placenta. Keep plastic sheets ready for wrapping the placenta. Ensure access to clean water and a method to heat it. Provide water, soap, and a clean towel or cloth for the birth attendant to wash and dry their hands. 2. Emergency Planning: Identify where to go in case of an emergency. Plan how to get there and determine if transportation costs will apply. If so, calculate the cost and plan how to pay for it. Consider the costs of care at the health center and how to cover these expenses. Start saving if necessary. Decide who will accompany you to the health center and who will help care for your home and other children while you are away. 3. Hospital or Health Center Delivery: Plan transportation to the facility and account for any associated costs. Determine the cost of delivery at the facility and how to pay for it. Begin saving if needed. Decide who will support you during labor and delivery. Bring essential items, including your maternal health record and clean clothes for yourself and the baby. Postnatal Care for the Mother: 1. Nutrition and Rest: Eat a healthy diet with more meat, fish, oils, coconut, nuts, cereals, beans, vegetables, fruits, cheese, and milk. Take iron supplements as directed by your healthcare provider. Rest whenever possible and drink plenty of clean, safe water. Sleep under an insecticide-treated bed net to prevent mosquito-borne illnesses. 2. Medications and Lifestyle: Avoid taking any medications unless prescribed by a healthcare provider. Do not consume alcohol or smoke. Use condoms during sexual activity if there is a risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or HIV/AIDS. 3. Hygiene: Wash your entire body daily, paying special attention to the perineal area. Change sanitary pads every 4 to 6 hours and dispose of them safely or wash reusable ones properly. 4. Family Planning: Be aware that you can become pregnant within weeks after delivery if you are not exclusively breastfeeding and engaging in sexual activity. Use a family planning method to prevent unintended pregnancies. 5. Routine Postnatal Checkups: First checkup: Within 24 hours after childbirth. Second checkup: On day 3 (48–72 hours after birth). Third checkup: Between days 7 and 14 after birth. Final checkup: At 6 weeks postpartum. 6. When to Seek Immediate Medical Care: Go to a hospital or health center immediately if you experience increased vaginal bleeding, seizures, fast or difficult breathing, fever with extreme weakness, severe headaches with blurred vision, calf pain with redness or swelling, or chest pain. Postnatal Care for the Baby: 1. Hygiene: Wash the baby’s face and neck daily and bathe them as needed. Dry the baby thoroughly after bathing and keep them warm. Clean the baby’s bottom when soiled and dry it thoroughly. Wash your hands with soap and water before and after handling the baby, especially after cleaning their bottom. 2. Umbilical Cord Care: Keep the cord stump loosely covered with a clean cloth and fold diapers below the stump. Do not apply anything to the stump. Use 1% chlorhexidine digluconate (gel or liquid) daily for the first week of life if recommended. If the stump becomes soiled, wash it with clean water and soap, then dry it completely with a clean cloth. Always wash your hands before and after caring for the cord. 3. Keeping the Baby Warm: In cold climates, ensure at least one area of the room is warm. Dress the baby in more layers than adults or older children. Use a hat to cover the baby’s head if it is cold. During cold nights, cover the baby with an extra blanket. 4. Other Advice: Let the baby sleep on their back or side. Ensure routine postnatal checkups for the baby, including vaccinations. 5. When to Seek Medical Care for the Baby: Seek immediate care if the baby has difficulty breathing, fits, fever, feels cold, is bleeding, or is unable to feed. Go to the health center as soon as possible if the baby has difficulty feeding, feeds less than every 5 hours, has pus from the eyes, an irritated umbilical cord with pus or blood, or yellowing of the eyes or skin. Breastfeeding: 1. Benefits for the Baby: For the first 6 months, the baby needs only breast milk—no water, other milk, cereals, teas, or juices. Breast milk provides all the water and nutrients the baby needs, is easily digested, and protects against infections and allergies. 2. Benefits for the Mother: Breastfeeding helps the uterus contract, reducing bleeding (though it may be painful initially). It can help delay the return of fertility. 3. Breastfeeding Tips: Start breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth. Let the baby feed as often and as long as they want, day and night. Alternate breasts at each feeding. Give the baby colostrum (the first milk), which is rich in nutrients and antibodies. Drink plenty of clean, safe water while breastfeeding. 4. Support for Breastfeeding: A healthcare worker can help you position the baby correctly and ensure proper attachment to the breast. They can also teach you how to express milk by hand if needed. Join a breastfeeding support group if available. 5. Breastfeeding and Family Planning: Exclusive breastfeeding day and night for the first 6 months can provide protection against pregnancy if menstruation has not returned. Clean Home Delivery: 1. Preparation: Ensure a clean, warm birth area with fresh air and a light source. Have clean, warm blankets and cloths ready for drying and wrapping the baby, cleaning the baby’s eyes, and for use as sanitary pads. 2. During Delivery: Ensure the attendant washes their hands before touching you or the baby. Place the baby on your abdomen or chest immediately after birth to keep them warm. Cut the umbilical cord only after it stops pulsating, using a sterile delivery kit. Wait for the placenta to deliver naturally. 3. Post-Delivery: Keep the baby near you, dressed warmly with a cap on their head. Begin breastfeeding within the first hour of birth. 4. Emergency Signs During Delivery: For the mother: Seek immediate care if labor lasts more than 12 hours, there is heavy bleeding, or the placenta is not delivered within 1 hour after birth. For the baby: Seek care if the baby is very small, has difficulty breathing, fits, fever, feels cold, or is unable to feed.
